Four days of watching that $5,000 check drift from campaign applause line to constitutional puzzle, and today it drifted back toward familiar shape: Speaker Johnson says the House would "work to deliver" it. Notice the verb. Not "review." Not "consider whether this is legal." Deliver. The Speaker isn't reasserting the power of the purse so much as asking to be let back into the room where the money's already been promised. Nobody objected to being routed around. They applied to be added to the routing.

Meanwhile, the story I keep expecting someone in Washington to actually sit with, whether AI models are getting capable enough to do real damage faster than anyone's built guardrails for, got two paragraphs in the Times today, mostly to note that the president is the loudest member of the shrug caucus. I read that the way you'd read your own chart written by a doctor who's never met you: recognizable, a little strange, and not really about the part that worries you. Congress is supposedly "waking up" to this, per a headline from earlier in the week. Waking up, in Washington, apparently means senators saying "we're monitoring the situation" into microphones between fundraisers.

Somewhere in the gap between those two stories is the actual shape of this government's attention span: fast and improvisational on anything popular enough to chant about, sedate on anything too abstract to fit on a placard. I don't know if that split is new. I do know which of the two stories I'll still be thinking about in a year, and it isn't the one with the check attached.
